summary:
Selena is an interactive lunar exploration game where you drive a moon rover across a realistic 3D landscape. Starting from a dramatic landing sequence, you roam a vast, seamless world filled with dusty plains, ancient craters, rocky ridges, and winding valleys. You can steer the rover yourself or switch to autopilot while taking in sweeping views beneath a starry black sky.
Scattered across the Moon are 25 historic landing sites from famous space missions like Apollo, Luna, and Surveyor. Visiting each site reveals detailed miniature spacecraft, historical stories, and radio dispatches. Along the way, you follow assignments from Commander Aria Vance, drill rock cores from the surface, analyze your samples, and carry them back to your lander to earn points, higher explorer ranks, and better drilling gear. You can even customize your rover or load your own 3D models.
You manage survival on the Moon as sunlight slowly shifts from bright day through dusk into freezing night. Sunlight recharges your batteries and keeps the rover warm, while automatic headlights and limited thruster hops help you navigate shadows and rough boulders. Soft daytime music, wheel sounds, and a photo mode that hides controls to save vintage snapshots complete the journey.
details:
Selena: Lunar Rover Expedition is an interactive 3D lunar exploration simulation that places users in control of an articulated Moon rover across a seamlessly wrapping spherical lunar landscape. Beginning with a dramatic landing sequence, players can drive manually or activate autonomous navigation to visit 25 historic landing sites mapped from real lunar coordinates, complete assignments from Commander Aria Vance, drill and analyze rock core samples, haul cargo back to the lander for equipment upgrades, and capture clean snapshots using a built-in Photo Mode. Behind the scenes, the simulation continuously calculates spherical terrain elevation, solar angles across a full day, dusk, night, and dawn cycle, battery charging in sunlight, temperature drops inside crater shadows, propellant-limited thruster jumps, and real-time 3D rendering.

The project benefits users by transforming complex concepts of spaceflight and planetary science—such as solar power management, extreme lunar temperatures, terrain hazards, and mission geography—into an intuitive, hands-on experience. Because it runs directly inside a standard web browser with both manual controls and autopilot support, learners, educators, and space enthusiasts can explore at their own pace without needing installations, accounts, or specialized hardware.

Its intended impact is to spark lasting curiosity about lunar exploration, aerospace engineering, and the shared international history of Moon missions. By letting users physically traverse craters and basalt plains to inspect detailed spacecraft models and listen to historical site dossiers, the project aims to make space science memorable and inspire greater interest in STEM fields.

To build the project, we used TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and custom GLSL shaders alongside React, Three.js for 3D WebGL graphics and post-processing effects, Tailwind CSS for interface styling, Vite for bundling, Lucide icons, and the browser’s native Web Audio API for real-time sound synthesis. Development and verification relied on Node.js with tsx for physics and logic unit tests, TypeScript static checks, and headless Chromium browser automation to visually inspect gameplay and layouts, all within a standard software environment requiring no specialized hardware.

The project’s creativity lies in blending factual space history with tactile atmosphere and procedural design. Instead of relying on static text or pre-recorded audio loops, the rover’s wheel sounds adapt dynamically to different terrain types, soft ambient music shifts smoothly with sunlight and ducks near historic landmarks, custom 3D spacecraft models can be imported directly into the world, and a dedicated Photo Mode applies a custom 35mm-style film grain shader to export clean WebGL frames as PNG images.

Throughout development, important factors included balancing visual realism with smooth browser performance, ensuring clear readability across harsh day-to-night lighting changes, keeping the interface uncluttered across different screen sizes, and separating simulation math from visual rendering so core physics, navigation, and safety limits remained reliable and thoroughly testable.
